_doc: THE MERGE QUEUE. The manager SCHEDULES merges; it does not resolve the
conflicts that not scheduling them causes.
⚠️ THIS FILE DID NOT EXIST UNTIL 2026-09-03, AND ITS ABSENCE IS THE POINT.
The day manager ran a merge queue that morning -- it declared an order, it
held sessions at position 2+, it promoted and poked -- and it worked. But it
existed only in that session's context. It was cited to a sub-session as
'the state of record ... created today', and a search of every branch and
every commit in the repo found NOTHING: not on main, not on any ref, not in
history. What existed was docs/runbooks/merge-queue.md, which is prose.
That is the exact failure the operator named on 2026-09-03: 'that's one of
the base functions of what a manager session is supposed to do. That needs
to be canonized. It's not something you take upon yourself in the session.'
A queue held in a session's head dies with that session, and the next
manager re-derives it from scratch -- or does not, and the morning repeats.
MEASURED HARM on the day the queue was invented, which is why it exists:
26 merges to main, 19 of them (73%) touching a shared register, five of
those the manager's own and two of THOSE bare lease heartbeats -- merges
whose entire content is a timestamp. Every one re-conflicted every open PR
touching a register. #10918 went dirty three times; #10923 the moment it
went green. Sessions burned ~16-minute pytest-runs that were void before
they finished.
THE INVARIANT THIS FILE EXISTS TO HOLD, and the one check_manager_scope.py
R8 enforces: AT MOST ONE ENTRY IS REBASING AT A TIME. Two sessions rebasing
against the same moving main is the thundering herd the queue prevents; it
is also the state that looks fine to each session individually, which is why
it needs a check rather than a convention.
PROMOTE AND POKE. A session does not poll. When position 1 lands, the
manager sets the next entry to `rebasing` AND messages that session. An
entry left `waiting` with nothing ahead of it is a session sitting idle for
a promotion nobody sent -- the 46-minute block the operator caught, in a
different costume.
STATES, NEVER COLLAPSED:
waiting   -- in the queue, not yet cleared to rebase. Do NOT rebase.
rebasing  -- cleared, and the ONLY entry that may be. At most one.
green     -- rebased, CI passed, waiting on the manager's merge click.
merged    -- landed. Keep the row until the next manager reads it.
blocked   -- cannot proceed; `blocked_on` says why. NOT `waiting`:
'not my turn' and 'cannot go' are different facts.
⚠️ `green` IS THE STATE THAT COST US. #10923 sat green and mergeable from
11:01:05Z to 11:11Z and the OPERATOR noticed before the mechanism did. The
manager's own 11:04Z sweep timer was enabled, carried next_run_at 11:04:00Z,
and never fired -- no error, no log. A cadence check that graded whether a
sweep was ARMED would have passed straight through that hole, because it WAS
armed. See check_manager_scope.py's R7 note for what is and is not covered.
